messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: (re)moving files in stan's tree
parts:
Can we establish a standard operating procedure for (re)moving files?

The problem is that if Alice has made changes to a file but is not
ready to push them yet, and Bob (not Carpenter specifically but the
Bob that is not Alice) decides to rename that file, move it to a
different directory, delete it, etc., then when Alice updates the
update fails or "succeeds" and the changes go poof. Subversion was not
designed to handle such things gracefully. Thus, the traditional
advice when using subversion is to "commit to the central repository
the instant you have made a change", which mitigates the potential for
this particular problem but leads to a lot of half-baked commits.

So, I think Alice needs to say on the list something like "I am going
to (re)move the following files from ... to ... in +24 hours, so
anyone should commit any uncommitted changes to those files by then or
petition for a delay."

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] (re)moving files in stan's tree
parts:
I've only ever used CVS or SVN. Google also
supports Mercurial, but not Git.

I was certainly taught that you need to commit
early and often so that merges become someone
else's problem.

This isn't just a problem for moving or
deleting files, but also for rearranging them
internally, which tends to mess up merges in a big
way.

Is there a better version control system than
SVN for handling the problem of person A changing
file X out from under person B's uncommitted changes?
I can't imagine how it could be handled other than
side-channel communication (barring mind reading).

I thought the main benefit of easy branch-and-merge
systems like Git or Mercurial is that you could keep
your own local work in version control until you were
ready to merge back to the main branch. That doesn't
solve the problem Ben outlines, though.

Joel Spolsky wrote a nice-looking tutorial on
Mercurial, comparing to SVN:

http://hginit.com/

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: (re)moving files in stan's tree
parts:
On Feb 8, 3:20 pm, Bob Carpenter <c...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> I've only ever used CVS or SVN.  Google also
> supports Mercurial, but not Git.

Google code doesn't support git directly, although since the last time
I complained about subversion, I started using git-svn. This basically
means I am using git locally and a bidirectional bridge between git
and svn to update, commit, etc. However, the bridge gets blown up when
files get (re)moved in the subversion repository.

> Is there a better version control system than
> SVN for handling the problem of person A changing
> file X out from under person B's uncommitted changes?
> I can't imagine how it could be handled other than
> side-channel communication (barring mind reading).

Git hashes all the files. So, if you

mv foo bar

and commit, bar has the same hash as foo and so git knows that edits
to bar stem from the history of foo. Hashing is critical for something
like the Linux kernel that has so many people who could potentially
move a file out from under someone else. As far as svn is concerned,
bar appears via immaculate conception.

I'm not strongly advocating switching to git, although I do think it
would have been a better choice to start with and maybe it is
something to think about after stan 1.0 is released. For now, I think
we could get by if disruptive changes were pre-announced with at least
24 hours notice.

Ben

> How do you feel about Mercurial?  It seems to
> provide the same advantages as Git, though
> I don't know about linking (it must be more than
> hashing if they want to guarantee no conflicts) files.

I have used Mercurial a little bit. It is popular for python projects
because python itself uses Mercurial. Almost everything post-
subversion supports local branches, so you can work on something (or
multiple things in multiple branches) and push when it is ready.

For a comparison on the the (re)moving issue see

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/1537616/handling-renames-svn-vs-git-vs-mercurial

> So if you continue editing your local foo and
> commit changes to it as if foo was still there,
> when you merge back it finds where bar went and
> tries to merge there?
Yes

> Often I find myself splitting foo into foo1 and foo2 and
> putting both in a subdirectory relative to the original foo
> (that's what happened with the densities in two steps).

I think that is supposed to be smooth but I've never done that
personally.

> > I'm not strongly advocating switching to git,
>
> Not an option as it's not supported by Google code.

There is the option of mandating everyone use git-svn, but mercurial
might be just as good for our purposes.

> What do you think of as a disruptive change?  Or perhaps
> more simply, what ISN'T a disruptive change?  Is it
> just something that'll disrupt a local merge?  So it'd
> include swapping order of functions in a file, renaming
> functions, etc.

Yeah, I'd say "likely to disrupt the merge" is disruptive, albeit
subjective. There are big parts of Stan that only Bob works on, so for
example, there is not much chance of his changes to the parser
disrupting someone else. Conversely, moving all the files in prob to
somewhere in univariate vs. multivariate and discrete vs. continuous
subfolders could have bitten anyone (and did bite me).

> How about what Daniel just did, which was a wholesale
> replacement of "unsigned int" with either "size_t"
> or "vector<T>::size_type" as appropriate?

That seems non-disruptive because it is unlikely anyone else would be
changing unsigned int to int, although it could happen. I would say
that changing files is usually non-disruptive and changing the file
structure is usually disruptive (unless you are just adding purely new
files).

There is no perfect solution, and even under git / hg / bzr etc. you
get merge conflicts where 2 people change the same part of the same
file in different ways. But the post-subversion VCS have mechanisms to
minimize and resolve merge conflicts.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: (re)moving files in stan's tree
parts:
Thanks for all the descriptions of Git and SVN.

I had no idea all this merging and renaming was handled
in Git and Mercurial. That seems like another major
advantage in addition to easy branch merging.

Everyone told me I had to change from CVS to SVN,
but other than smoother handling of binaries, I
haven't noticed much difference.

I'd personally rather just migrate to Mercurial
than try to tie git to SVN. But maybe it's easier
to install/maintain than I'm imagining.

- Bob
